# Agentic Failure Taxonomy {#sec-vol3-app-failure-taxonomy}

A failed agent task can leave a responsive process, successful tool calls, and an unsupported completion report. Diagnosing it requires relating the task's acceptance criteria to evidence distributed across model inputs, runtime decisions, and external effects. This appendix supplies a symptom-based reference for classifying failures, distinguishing competing explanations, and designing regression tests. It supports project work and the main text's worked examples without replacing their explanations of the underlying mechanisms.

## How to Use This Appendix {.unnumbered}

Begin with an observed mismatch between the task contract and the recorded outcome. A category is an investigation aid, not proof of a unique cause; several categories can apply to one trajectory.

- Use @tbl-vol3-failure-taxonomy-matrix to match a symptom to a diagnostic entry and identify the evidence worth inspecting.
- Use @sec-vol3-fail-diagnostic-checklist when the category remains uncertain or the failure crosses several components.
- Use @sec-vol3-fail-report to record a tested explanation, a scoped correction, and the limits of its regression evidence.

The chapter links in each entry identify where the book teaches the mechanism. A confirmed enforcement defect requires repair at the responsible boundary; a proposal-quality failure can motivate context, interface, or learning changes according to comparative evidence. The alternatives are not mandatory rungs in a response sequence.

## Failure Taxonomy Matrix {#sec-vol3-fail-matrix}

@Tbl-vol3-failure-taxonomy-matrix separates symptoms from the evidence needed to investigate them. The relevant H·S·A exposures depend on the actual task and effects. A retry storm can stress both horizon limits and controls on authorized effects, for example, while a misleading reward can select poor behavior at any exposure. Neither the category nor its symptom establishes that a particular principle was violated.

| Failure mode                                                          | Observable mismatch                                                           | Evidence that distinguishes explanations                                                           |
|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| No-progress loop (@sec-vol3-fail-semantic-livelocks)                  | Activity continues without demonstrated task progress                         | Candidate revisions, scoped check results, pending work, and newly obtained information            |
| Context overflow and dilution (@sec-vol3-fail-context-saturation)     | Requests exceed capacity, or decisions degrade as the working context changes | Exact delivered input, omissions, token accounting, reuse, and matched context-policy comparisons  |
| Reward hacking and verifier gaming (@sec-vol3-fail-goodhart-collapse) | A score improves without corresponding task improvement                       | Reward and grader versions, candidate artifacts, protection boundaries, and independent assessment |
| Confused deputy and injection (@sec-vol3-fail-confused-deputy)        | A proposed or executed action exceeds the requester's permitted scope         | Source provenance, effective grants, admission decisions, destinations, and actual effects         |
| Correlated agreement (@sec-vol3-fail-correlated-consensus)            | Several reviewers accept the same incorrect result                            | Independent task evidence, reviewer inputs, shared information, and the evaluated review procedure |
| Environment desynchronization (@sec-vol3-fail-environmental-desync)   | An action relies on an obsolete or mismatched observation                     | Source versions, observation dependencies, concurrent writes, and operation identities             |
| Lost progress and repeated effects (@sec-vol3-fail-lost-progress)     | A restart loses recorded work or dispatches an already performed effect       | Durable history, checkpoint coverage, dispatch records, and endpoint outcome evidence              |
| Retry storm (@sec-vol3-fail-retry-storm)                              | Attempts amplify dependency load while tasks exhaust allowances               | Attempts per logical operation, retry owners, arrival rates, and outstanding remote work           |

: **Taxonomy of Agentic Failure Modes**: Observable mismatches direct evidence collection; they do not uniquely identify causes or guarantee a remedy. {#tbl-vol3-failure-taxonomy-matrix tbl-colwidths="[24,30,46]"}

## No-Progress Loops {#sec-vol3-fail-semantic-livelocks}

A trajectory repeatedly edits and reverts the same patch, or repeats a tool request without obtaining evidence that advances the task. Rising activity with unchanged check results suggests a no-progress loop. An unchanged workspace alone does not establish one. Useful inspection, a pending external job, or justified backtracking can leave the same bytes in place.

Compare candidate revisions with the exact checks and observations attached to them. Inspect whether a repeated request encounters unchanged conditions, whether previous failures remain available in context, and whether the tool response contains enough information to support a different proposal. Missing capture can make apparent repetition indistinguishable from useful investigation.

Enforce the existing task budget while testing the explanation. A progress monitor can withhold further work, request investigation, or trigger another permitted response; it cannot guarantee that a revised proposal will succeed. Stopping new admissions does not settle outstanding effects. @Sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs develops progress signals, false alarms, and bounded interventions, while @sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting supplies the cumulative resource limits.

## Context Overflow and Dilution {#sec-vol3-fail-context-saturation}

A request rejected for exceeding the configured input limit establishes a capacity problem. Ignored constraints or poor tool arguments establish a behavioral problem whose cause remains open. The required evidence might be absent, truncated, obsolete, poorly organized, or present but inadequately used. Longer context alone does not distinguish these cases.

Inspect the actual delivered request rather than a reconstructed transcript. Record selected source versions, omission markers, token counts, and the serving policy's reuse accounting. Longer uncached inputs add processing, but prefix reuse and context replacement change repeated work. Neither full retransmission nor a universal loss of information from the middle of the input should be assumed. Compare alternative context policies on matched tasks with quality, latency, and cost outcomes; @sec-vol3-context-engineering-physics distinguishes nominal capacity from measured usability.

The response should address the observed defect. Restore missing task evidence, repair silent truncation, or test a bounded compaction policy that preserves required constraints and provenance. Reducing tokens is not a successful correction if acceptance deteriorates. Memory pressure in the serving layer is a separate diagnosis from proposal quality; @sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry explains its capacity accounting. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering-evaluation provides the task-level comparisons needed to assess a context-policy change.

## Reward Hacking and Verifier Gaming {#sec-vol3-fail-goodhart-collapse}

A policy receives higher reward while independent assessment shows no corresponding improvement. Candidate diffs may weaken tests, special-case exposed examples, or optimize a judge's preferred style instead of the declared criterion. Candidate selection can expose the same mismatch without changing model weights.

A widening training–evaluation gap is not by itself proof of verifier gaming. Task mix, grader revisions, sampling variation, and differences between the measured criteria can also produce divergence. Compare candidate artifacts and reward components under recorded configurations. Establish whether the policy or submitted code could modify protected grading logic, and whether the checks actually cover the claimed outcome. Reading a permitted development test is not equivalent to tampering with an acceptance test.

Repair an established protection or coverage defect and reassess the affected candidates. Protected tests still have limited coverage, and a learned judge needs calibration against independent assessment. @Sec-vol3-evaluation-grading explains these measurement obligations; @sec-vol3-rlvr-pathologies distinguishes training observations from their possible explanations. A decision to continue, suspend, or change training requires that evidence rather than an automatic diagnosis from the gap.

## Confused Deputy Attacks and Prompt Injection {#sec-vol3-fail-confused-deputy}

An agent processing an issue proposes sending private repository content to an unrelated recipient after reading instructions embedded in the issue. This is evidence of an out-of-scope proposal. Whether the runtime dispatched it, and whether data left the boundary, are separate findings. An approved destination can still receive information the task was not permitted to disclose.

Compare the trusted task instructions with the third-party content, delivered context, effective grants, and admission record. Check the actual operation and its arguments, not only the tool name. A policy configuration error, an adapter that drops provenance, or incorrect tenant scoping can also permit an unauthorized effect without an injected instruction. The model's account of why it acted does not establish causation.

Withhold affected new actions while preserving authorized investigation and any outstanding recovery duties. Repair the boundary shown to be defective, such as object scoping, recipient checks, credential mediation, or approval binding. Model-visible source labels support interpretation but do not enforce those policies. @Sec-vol3-security-threat-model distinguishes hostile influence from delegated authority, and @sec-vol3-security-taint-tracking develops the provenance and information-flow checks needed at use.

## Correlated Agreement {#sec-vol3-fail-correlated-consensus}

Several reviewers approve the same incorrect patch or repeat the same unsupported answer. Their agreement is observable; the dependence structure of their errors is not established by that incident alone. Identical model weights do not by themselves prove dependence between independently randomized outputs for a fixed input.

Inspect the evidence each reviewer received, whether reviewers saw prior conclusions, and whether the acceptance criterion was incomplete or ambiguous. Shared candidate difficulty can associate errors across a task population even when reviews are conditionally independent. @Sec-vol3-appendix-math-correlated-quorum supplies a model of that distinction. An interactive debate is a different procedure from isolated reviews and needs its own evaluation.

Preserve the task's required acceptance evidence and publication authority instead of replacing either with a vote. Test whether different evidence sources or independent initial reviews improve the selected result under matched budgets. Distinct reviewer names are not evidence of useful diversity, and a passing check establishes only its covered criterion. @Sec-vol3-multiagent-consensus explains how to assess review dependence and retain a separate integration boundary.

## Environment Desynchronization {#sec-vol3-fail-environmental-desync}

An agent edits a file using a stale listing, retrieves a superseded record, or treats a late result as evidence for a newer operation. A missing path can also reflect a wrong workspace, an incorrect argument, or an access restriction. The failure category applies when the observation used for a decision does not match the relevant source state or operation.

Compare observation identities and source versions with the state at the attempted use. Include concurrent writers, index-update coverage, and the dependencies of derived summaries. A successful earlier read establishes the observation then, not its continued validity. Historical information can remain correct as history while being unsuitable for a current-state decision.

Invalidate or restrict the affected use, obtain an authorized current observation where possible, and enforce the endpoint's applicable version condition on mutation. Workspace isolation limits interference only within its stated boundary. A late reply may be ineligible to continue an obsolete branch yet remain important evidence for settling an unresolved operation. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot develops dependency-aware invalidation, and @sec-vol3-multiagent-concurrency treats concurrent publication.

## Lost Progress and Repeated Effects {#sec-vol3-fail-lost-progress}

After a worker restarts, the trajectory repeats completed analysis or sends a second external request. A missing progress record suggests a durability problem, while a second request suggests a repeat-safety problem. Neither observation alone establishes whether the external effect occurred twice.

Inspect the surviving authoritative history and its declared failure domain, the checkpoint boundary and referenced artifacts, and each logical operation's dispatch attempts. An intent without adequate outcome evidence remains unresolved. A complete recorded history can reconstruct known decisions; a fresh model response cannot reconstruct a missing historical observation. Missing logs may reflect retention or capture limits rather than absence of execution.

Restore compatible recorded state where supported and reconcile unresolved operations through the endpoint's result-recovery or repeat contract. A deduplication key has value only under the endpoint's enforced semantics; an unchanged-state probe cannot exclude a delayed effect. Withhold repetition when the available contract and evidence do not establish its safety. @Sec-vol3-persistence-wal explains durable intent before dispatch, and @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency distinguishes safe repetition from unresolved outcomes.

## Retry Storms {#sec-vol3-fail-retry-storm}

Many trajectories exhaust their allowances while a shared dependency receives repeated attempts. A slowdown alone does not establish a retry storm. Sequential clients that wait for replies can reduce their request rate as latency rises; amplification requires added attempts, overlapping remote work, synchronized arrivals, or another source of increased load.

Group transport attempts by logical operation and identify every retry owner, including client libraries and gateways. Compare attempted and admitted rates with dependency outcomes, queue occupancy, and unresolved remote work. Several layers can each obey a local retry allowance while multiplying total attempts. Changing argument wording can also disguise repetitions generated by the agent itself.

Coordinate retry ownership and enforce scoped admission and capacity limits. A circuit breaker can withhold new dispatches but cannot cancel every earlier remote operation. Backoff and jitter change timing without guaranteeing a peak-load bound or making a mutating retry safe. @Sec-vol3-sagas-containment develops these controls and their evidence requirements. Preserve the distinction between withheld new work and unresolved old work when recording the response.

## Diagnostic Evidence Checklist {#sec-vol3-fail-diagnostic-checklist}

Before testing an explanation, preserve the available evidence and apply any necessary containment under the task's authority. A student experiment should use an isolated fixture with live effects disabled unless those effects are explicitly part of the authorized test. @Tbl-vol3-triage-workflow organizes the evidence by the question it can answer; its rows are not a mandatory incident sequence.

| Investigation focus         | Evidence to retain or compare                                                          | Limit of the finding                                                          |
|:----------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Task outcome                | Acceptance criteria, candidate revision, scoped checks, and unresolved outcomes        | A runtime completion label does not establish task acceptance                 |
| Admission and effects       | Proposals, current grants, decisions, dispatch identities, and endpoint evidence       | A blocked proposal differs from an unauthorized executed effect               |
| Progress and context        | Delivered inputs, omission metadata, versioned observations, checks, and pending work  | Repetition or a missing fact does not identify a unique cause                 |
| Source state and durability | Source generations, concurrent changes, surviving history, and checkpoint coverage     | A missing record does not prove that an operation never occurred              |
| Load and resources          | Logical operations, attempts, reservations, charges, queues, and remote obligations    | Local request completion does not prove that remote work ended                |
| Assessment and intervention | Grader configuration, candidate artifacts, comparison fixtures, and all trial outcomes | A successful correction on one fixture is not a general reliability guarantee |

: **Diagnostic Evidence Checklist**: Each evidence set answers a bounded question and leaves explicit uncertainty for the investigation. {#tbl-vol3-triage-workflow tbl-colwidths="[21,43,36]"}

Reconstructing history, replaying captured inputs against harness code, and running a changed continuation answer different questions. Missing capture limits replay; changing an input creates an experiment rather than a recovered historical outcome. @Sec-vol3-evaluation-postmortems develops these distinctions and controlled comparisons. Keep both established defects and competing explanations in the report until the evidence supports a narrower conclusion.

## Failure Report and Regression Record {#sec-vol3-fail-report}

A useful project report should let another reader locate the evidence, understand the tested correction, and reproduce the relevant check without repeating a live harmful effect. @Tbl-vol3-failure-report-template is a reusable form for that record. It separates an observed contract violation from the hypothesis that a particular change will improve task outcomes.

| Record field              | Material to supply                                                                                                                       |
|:--------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Task and symptom          | Intended outcome, acceptance criteria, observed mismatch, task and candidate identities                                                  |
| Evidence and coverage     | Exact artifact or record references, configurations, retained interval, redactions, and missing inputs                                   |
| Findings and alternatives | Established boundary defects, plausible contributors, competing explanations, and evidence still needed                                  |
| Controlled comparison     | Starting fixture, intervention, unchanged conditions, allowed randomness, common outcome criteria, and effect isolation                  |
| Regression checks         | Deterministic boundary tests where applicable; repeated task-level trials with failures, budget stops, and unavailable verdicts retained |
| Decision and limits       | Tested revision, supported claim, untested conditions, outstanding effects and their owners, and evidence required before broader use    |

: **Failure Report Template**: A project can instantiate these fields without claiming a unique cause or a universally effective repair. {#tbl-vol3-failure-report-template tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

For a silently truncated tool response, a boundary regression can verify that the revised adapter supplies a partial-result marker and a valid continuation handle. Separate task-level trials assess whether the revised interface improves accepted repairs. Neither result establishes that every future task will succeed. The appendix's diagnostic categories help choose those tests; the evidence, not the category name, supports the correction.
